content: Patients, particularly those living with HIV (PLHIV), would benefit from a rapid point-of-care test to diagnose tuberculosis (TB). It is recommended that testing using Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 2 be conducted simultaneously. Algorithms 3 and 4 are subsequent steps following Algorithm 1, with the pathway determined by the rifampicin (RIF) resistance result. Algorithm 3 is designed for patients with confirmed rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) and focuses on providing additional rapid drug susceptibility testing (DST). Available options include first-line line-probe assays (FL-LPA), second-line line-probe assays (SL-LPA), and recently recommended low-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs). Both test groups yield similar DST results, but the low-complexity automated NAATs are simpler to perform, can be used regardless of smear grade, and are better suited for decentralized settings. Rapid early detection of fluoroquinolone (FQ) resistance in multidrug-resistant (MDR)/RR-TB patients is critical, and low-complexity automated NAATs are the preferred option for scaling up and improving access. A new molecular test for pyrazinamide (PZA) resistance is recommended, which belongs to the high-complexity reverse hybridization NAAT class. Currently, this test is recommended for use only on isolates, with testing performed at higher levels of the laboratory network for selected patients. An interconnected laboratory network offering a range of tests may best address patient needs. Algorithm 4 is a follow-up algorithm for patients with RIF-susceptible TB. It aims to detect isoniazid (INH) resistance (if INH testing was not included in Algorithm 1) or FQ resistance when isoniazid-resistant TB (Hr-TB) has been identified using moderate-complexity automated NAATs in Algorithm 1. Currently, INH detection is not widely implemented at the initial diagnosis stage, but this will change with the adoption of moderate-complexity automated NAATs as initial tests that also detect INH resistance. The adoption of low-complexity automated NAATs for follow-up testing of RIF-susceptible TB could also enhance the detection of INH resistance. The estimated incidence of Hr-TB is higher than that of RR-TB, and both require modifications to the treatment regimen. Hr-TB patients would need the addition of an FQ to their therapy. For patients diagnosed using a moderate-complexity automated NAAT that detects both RIF and INH resistance in Algorithm 1, there are two options for FQ resistance detection: low-complexity automated NAATs, which are simpler and can be decentralized, or SL-LPA, which, although more complex, may already be available in the same laboratory as the moderate-complexity automated NAAT. In settings or subpopulations with a high burden of Hr-TB, follow-up testing using low-complexity automated NAATs is appropriate, as it is simpler and more cost-effective than performing both FL-LPA and SL-LPA. Algorithm 1 is the preferred approach for testing to support the diagnosis of TB in individuals being evaluated for pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB and to achieve universal DST. This algorithm aligns with the goals of the End TB Strategy for the use of molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs) and universal DST. It is designed to be used with any of the mWRDs for detecting Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC), such as Xpert MTB/RIF, Xpert Ultra, Truenat MTB, Truenat MTB Plus, and TB-LAMP. However, the algorithm may need to be adapted depending on the specific mWRD used and the population being tested. In settings with a well-functioning referral system and a high risk of Hr-TB, a moderate-complexity automated NAAT may be preferred as the initial test due to its ability to simultaneously test for INH and RIF resistance. This algorithm is feasible when mWRD testing can be conducted on-site or accessed through a reliable referral system with short turnaround times.
